sections.h2: How is property tax set in New Jersey?
sections.html:
New Jersey property tax is a local tax based on value, and the State does not keep any of it. The Division of Taxation explains that real property is assessed at "true value" as of October 1 of the year before the tax year, and that all 21 counties have set the assessment level at 100 percent. The 566 taxing districts are then equalized so that county and school costs are shared fairly.

A town's general tax rate comes from dividing the money its budget needs by the total assessed value of its taxable property. Your bill is that rate multiplied by your assessment. Because the amount comes out of county, municipal and school budgets, a homeowner cannot appeal the tax itself, only the assessment on which the bill is built.

sections.h2: When are New Jersey property taxes due and what happens if they are late?
sections.html:
Bills are paid in four installments each year, on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Taxes are a continuous lien on the real estate, so an unpaid balance stays with the house through a sale.

The Division of Local Government Services guide to tax sales states that delinquent amounts may accrue interest of up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent on anything above that. If the delinquency passes $10,000 at the end of the municipal fiscal year, a year-end penalty of up to 6 percent may be added. Ask your municipal tax collector for the exact rate and the current payoff figure, since each town sets its own interest policy within those limits.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a New Jersey property assessment?
sections.html:
Appeal the assessment to your County Board of Taxation, and file before the deadline. The Division's Guide to Tax Appeal Hearings says appeals must be filed each year on or before April 1, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of assessment notices, and by May 1 where a municipality completed a revaluation or reassessment. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties follow an alternate calendar with a January 15 deadline.

The burden of proof is on the owner. The county board compares true market value to the assessed value, and the owner should present evidence from before the October 1 assessment date. Useful steps:

  • attach comparable sales of three to five similar properties to the petition when it is filed
  • add photographs of the subject property and the comparables
  • send copies of the comparables to the assessor and the tax board at least seven days before the hearing
  • attend the hearing, because non-appearance can lead to a judgment for lack of prosecution and block a later appeal to the Tax Court

Commercial owners must also file an income statement. Assessments of similar properties are not usable evidence, so rely on sales.

sections.h2: What is the common level range test?
sections.html:
It is the yardstick that decides whether your assessment is out of line with the rest of your town. The Division says that to prove an assessment excessive or discriminatory, an owner must show it fails either the True Market Value Standard or the Common Level Range Standard. The range is plus or minus 15 percent of the Director's Ratio for the taxing district, which is the average assessment-to-value percentage published for that municipality.

If the evidence shows your ratio is above the range, the taxable value is reset by applying the district's average ratio to your property's true value. A successful appeal also triggers the Freeze Act, which holds the assessed value in place for the assessment year and the two years after it, unless a revaluation or an added assessment changes things.

sections.h2: Which property tax relief programs can New Jersey homeowners use?
sections.html:
ANCHOR is the main homeowner benefit. The Division's benefit schedule pays homeowners with 2025 income of $150,000 or less $1,500, and those with income from $150,001 to $250,000 receive $1,000. Renters get $450, or $700 at age 65 and older. Payments start on a rolling basis on September 15, usually within 90 days of filing, and the total of all relief a person receives cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the main home.

The Senior Freeze program reimburses eligible seniors and disabled persons for tax increases on their principal residence, and the Stay NJ credit program uses the same combined application. The filing deadline for the 2025 application was November 2, 2026, and it has passed. Property tax deductions for senior citizens, disabled persons and veterans are also counted in the benefit cap. The Division's property tax relief FAQs list the current application steps.

sections.h2: What does a New Jersey tax sale mean for a homeowner?
sections.html:
A tax sale puts a lien up for auction, not the house itself. The state guide says all 566 municipalities must hold at least one tax sale a year if they have delinquent taxes or municipal charges. The buyer receives a tax sale certificate, and bidders bid the interest rate down from 18 percent; at one percent, bidders offer a premium instead.

The owner can still redeem the certificate by paying what is owed, plus a redemption penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent depending on the certificate amount. After two years, the certificate holder can start a foreclosure action in Superior Court, and if it succeeds the deed passes to the lien holder. Contact the tax collector long before a sale date to learn the sale schedule.

sections.h2: What should a seller do when property tax is owed in New Jersey?
sections.html: Ask the municipal tax collector for a written payoff that includes current installments, interest and any municipal charges, and ask whether the town has scheduled a tax sale. Share the figure with the title agent so it is paid out of the closing. A buyer paying cash can often close before a tax sale date, which ends the lien exposure.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my New Jersey property tax bill?
faqs.a: No, only the assessment can be appealed. The tax comes from municipal, county and school budgets and cannot be challenged. File the assessment appeal with your County Board of Taxation by April 1, or the date that applies to your county or revaluation.

faqs.q: What is the New Jersey property tax appeal deadline?
faqs.a: April 1 in most counties, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of assessment notices. It is May 1 where a municipal revaluation or reassessment occurred, and January 15 in Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties.

faqs.q: How much is the ANCHOR benefit for homeowners?
faqs.a: For the 2025 application it is $1,500 for homeowners with income of $150,000 or less and $1,000 for income of $150,001 to $250,000. Above $250,000 a homeowner is not eligible. The application deadline was November 2, 2026.

faqs.q: What interest does New Jersey charge on late property tax?
faqs.a: Up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 delinquent and up to 18 percent on the amount above that. A delinquency over $10,000 at the end of the fiscal year can also draw a penalty of up to 6 percent.

faqs.q: Can the state take my house for unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Eventually, through the lien process. The municipality sells a tax sale certificate, not the title. The certificate holder may begin a Superior Court foreclosure after two years if the certificate has not been redeemed.
